Introduction to the exercise & safety

In this experiment, you will determine the caffeine concentration in a beverage of your choice using solid phase extraction (SPE) for sample preparation, gas chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (GC-MS) for detection, and external calibration for quantification. You will also evaluate the recovery of your extraction process by spiking a sample with a caffeine standard. You will work in pairs throughout this experiment.

By the end of this lab, you should be able to:

1. Perform a complete SPE workflow on a reversed-phase C18 cartridge
2. Operate a GC-MS system with appropriate method parameters
3. Build and critically evaluate an external calibration curve
4. Calculate recovery from a standard spiking experiment
5. Identify and discuss sources of analytical error in the overall process
6. Write a scientific introduction on an assigned topic

Each pair of students will prepare one sample and one spiked sample, and by the end of the second day, present a short flash talk (~5 min) on one analytical error of the method. You will also write a scientific introduction on an assigned topic, leading to the aim of this experiment.

Solid phase extraction (SPE)

SPE is the sample preparation technique you'll use to prepare your beverage sample before GC-MS analysis. The fundamental problem is this: your beverages are water-based, and water has to be kept out of the GC-MS (section 1 explains why). SPE solves this by transferring caffeine out of the aqueous matrix and into an organic solvent (acetonitrile) that is GC-compatible. Along the way, SPE also removes interfering matrix components. SPE can concentrate an analyte as well, but you won't use it that way: your drinks contain plenty of caffeine and the GC-MS is very sensitive, so here the extract actually ends up more dilute than the drink. Getting rid of the water is the essential first step. Understanding why each step matters will help you troubleshoot problems in the lab.

Work through the numbered sections below in order, then complete the concept checks at the bottom.Work through the screens in order; the concept checks come at the end of the chapter.

Solid phase extraction is a sample preparation technique that uses a solid adsorbent (packed in a small cartridge) to selectively isolate target analytes from a complex sample matrix. Think of it as a selective filter: your beverage contains sugars, proteins, pigments, and hundreds of other compounds, but you only care about caffeine.

The critical reason we need SPE in this experiment is solvent exchange: your samples are aqueous (water-based), but GC requires the analyte to be dissolved in a volatile organic solvent. Water injected into a GC would damage the column and make separation impossible. SPE lets us trap caffeine from the water, wash away the aqueous matrix, and then elute caffeine into acetonitrile, a solvent the GC can handle. Beyond this essential solvent exchange, SPE also (1) removes interfering matrix components that would obscure your GC-MS signal, (2) can concentrate an analyte so it's above the detection limit, and (3) improves reproducibility compared to liquid-liquid extraction.

In this experiment, you'll use a CHROMABOND C18 ec cartridge, a reversed-phase adsorbent. The C18 (octadecyl) chains are nonpolar, so they retain nonpolar and moderately polar molecules like caffeine from an aqueous sample.

There are two general approaches in SPE, depending on the chemistry of your analyte and matrix:

Strategy 1: Retain the analyte: The analyte adsorbs onto the sorbent while interfering matrix components flow through. After a wash step, the analyte is eluted with a stronger solvent. This is what you'll do with caffeine on C18.

Strategy 2: Retain the interferences: The analyte flows through the cartridge while unwanted matrix components stick to the sorbent. The analyte is collected directly in the flow-through. This approach is used when matrix components are more strongly retained than the analyte.

Choosing between these strategies depends on the polarity of the analyte relative to the matrix and the sorbent chemistry. Reversed-phase sorbents like C18 retain nonpolar and moderately polar analytes from aqueous samples. Caffeine is moderately polar, so it is held well enough for Strategy 1 to work with water-based beverages.

Your CHROMABOND C18 ec cartridge (1 mL / 100 mg) consists of a small polypropylene syringe barrel packed with 100 mg of silica-based sorbent, held in place by two polyethylene frits (filter elements) at the top and bottom.

The sorbent: Silica particles are chemically bonded with C18 (18-carbon) alkyl chains. These long hydrocarbon chains create a nonpolar surface. When an aqueous sample passes through, nonpolar and moderately polar molecules (like caffeine) partition out of the water and onto the C18 surface via hydrophobic interactions (van der Waals forces).

The "ec" designation stands for "endcapped," meaning residual silanol groups on the silica surface have been chemically capped. This reduces unwanted secondary interactions (e.g., with basic compounds) and improves reproducibility.

The cartridge connects to the vacuum manifold via a Luer fitting, a standardized taper that ensures a leak-free seal.

A vacuum manifold allows you to process multiple SPE cartridges simultaneously. It consists of a rectangular glass chamber with a polypropylene lid that holds the cartridges on top. Test tubes or collection vessels sit inside the chamber below the cartridges.

How it works: A vacuum pump reduces the pressure inside the chamber. This pressure differential draws liquid through the cartridge from top to bottom. The control valve on the side lets you adjust the vacuum level, and each cartridge position in the lid has its own small valve, so you can start and stop the flow through each cartridge separately.

Why vacuum? Gravity alone is often too slow and inconsistent. The vacuum provides controlled, reproducible flow rates. You'll aim for about 1–2 drops per second. Consistent flow is critical because too fast a flow can reduce the contact time between analyte and sorbent, lowering recovery.

Key practical point: Always close the cartridge's valve first, add your solvent/sample to the cartridge, then carefully open the valve to start flow. This prevents sudden surges that could damage the sorbent bed or cause channeling.

Concept checks. Expand each question below and test your understanding before moving on.
Q Concept check 1: SPE sorbent drying
Why must you avoid letting the SPE sorbent bed run dry between conditioning and sample loading?
The polypropylene cartridge barrel undergoes stress cracking when exposed to air, compromising the seal between the sorbent bed and the barrel walls
Exposure to air causes oxidative degradation of the silica support, dissolving the bonded C18 chains and permanently destroying the sorbent bed
Air channels form in the sorbent bed, reducing contact between sample and sorbent, and the C18 chains may de-wet, losing their ability to retain analytes
A dry sorbent bed creates excess back-pressure that overloads the vacuum manifold pump, potentially damaging the diaphragm and causing uneven flow across cartridge positions
Correct! When the sorbent dries out, the C18 alkyl chains can collapse and become non-wettable again. Additionally, air trapped in the sorbent creates channels where the sample flows preferentially, bypassing most of the sorbent material. This drastically reduces retention efficiency and can ruin your recovery. If it happens, you need to start the conditioning process from scratch.
Q Concept check 2: SPE retention mechanism
In this experiment you use a C18 (reversed-phase) sorbent with an aqueous sample. What is the primary interaction mechanism retaining caffeine on the sorbent?
Ion exchange: caffeine becomes protonated in the aqueous sample and binds electrostatically to negatively charged silanol sites on the silica surface
Hydrophobic (van der Waals) interactions: caffeine partitions onto the nonpolar C18 surface to escape the aqueous phase
Hydrogen bonding: caffeine's carbonyl oxygens and ring nitrogens form strong H-bonds with residual silanol groups on the silica backbone
Size exclusion: caffeine's small molecular radius allows it to enter the silica pore network where larger matrix molecules cannot follow
Correct! Reversed-phase SPE relies on hydrophobic interactions. The long C18 alkyl chains create a nonpolar surface. When an aqueous sample passes through, molecules with enough nonpolar character, like caffeine, preferentially partition from the polar water phase onto the nonpolar sorbent surface via van der Waals forces. This is the same principle as reversed-phase HPLC. Caffeine, while moderately polar, has sufficient hydrophobic character (the fused purine ring system) to be retained on C18 from an aqueous sample.
Answer both concept checks before continuing.

GC-MS fundamentals

Gas chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry is the analytical technique you'll use to detect and quantify caffeine. The GC separates the mixture into individual compounds over time; the MS further separates ions by mass-to-charge ratio and detects them. Identification of compounds is then performed during data analysis by matching mass spectra against reference libraries.

Work through the numbered sections below in order, then complete the concept checks at the bottom.Work through the screens in order; the concept checks come at the end of the chapter.

Gas chromatography (GC) separates volatile compounds in a mixture. The principle is simple: a liquid sample is injected into a hot inlet where it vaporizes. A carrier gas (helium in your experiment) sweeps the vapor into a long, thin column coated on the inside with a chemical film (the stationary phase).

As the vaporized compounds travel through the column, they interact with the stationary phase. Compounds with stronger affinity for the stationary phase move more slowly; compounds with weaker affinity move faster. This differential migration separates the mixture into individual components that exit the column at different retention times.

Your column: HP-5MS Ultra Inert, 30 m × 0.25 mm ID × 0.25 µm film, a (5%-phenyl)-methylpolysiloxane stationary phase. This is a general-purpose, low-polarity column suitable for a wide range of analytes including caffeine.

Your method parameters: Injection in split mode (50:1; 30:1 when the instrument is less sensitive), 1 µL injection volume, helium carrier gas at 2.5 mL/min, oven temperature programmed from 120 °C (1 min hold) → 30 °C/min → 270 °C (3 min hold). Total run time: 9 minutes.

The inlet (injector): Set to 250 °C, hot enough to instantly vaporize your sample. The "split" mode (ratio 50:1) means that for every 1 part of the vaporized sample that enters the column, 50 parts are vented through the split vent. This prevents column overload for concentrated samples and sharpens peaks. A lower ratio (30:1) sends more caffeine onto the column; we use it when the instrument is less sensitive.

Temperature programming: Rather than holding the oven at a constant temperature, you ramp it upward. This is crucial because different compounds have different boiling points. Starting low allows volatile compounds to separate cleanly; ramping up pushes higher-boiling compounds off the column in a reasonable time. Without a temperature ramp, high-boiling compounds would emerge as extremely broad, undetectable peaks.

Carrier gas: Helium is inert, so it does not react with your compounds or the column, and it gives fast, efficient separations. It also suits the MS: helium's ion (m/z 4) lies far below your scan range (m/z 45–200), so it adds nothing to your spectra. The constant flow of 2.5 mL/min keeps compound transport the same all through the temperature program.

Why do we need GC separation before MS? A mass spectrometer would be overwhelmed by an unseparated mixture. Ions from different compounds would overlap, making identification and quantification impossible. GC delivers compounds one at a time (ideally) to the MS.

Step 2: Set GC method parameters




: 1



Oven: 120 °C

After the GC column, compounds enter the mass selective detector (MSD), a single-quadrupole mass spectrometer. The key steps are ionization, mass filtering, and detection.

Ionization (EI at 70 eV): Compounds are bombarded by a beam of high-energy electrons (70 eV) from a heated filament. This is called Electron Ionization (EI). The electron impact knocks an electron out of the analyte molecule, creating a positively charged radical cation (the molecular ion, M⁺·). The excess energy also causes reproducible fragmentation, breaking the molecule into characteristic fragment ions. This fragmentation pattern is like a molecular fingerprint.

The vacuum system: The analyzer operates under high vacuum (maintained by a foreline + turbo/diffusion pump). Without high vacuum, ions would collide with air molecules and never reach the detector. The mean free path of ions must be long enough for them to travel the length of the quadrupole.

The quadrupole mass filter: Four parallel metal rods with combined DC and RF (radio frequency) voltages. At any given voltage setting, only ions of one specific m/z (mass-to-charge ratio) have a stable trajectory through the rods and reach the detector. All other ions collide with the rods and are lost. By rapidly scanning through different voltages, the quadrupole sequentially allows different m/z values to pass.

The detector (HED + electron multiplier): Ions exiting the quadrupole strike a high-energy conversion dynode, producing secondary electrons that are amplified by an electron multiplier. The resulting electrical signal is proportional to the number of ions, and thus to the amount of analyte.

Scan mode: The quadrupole sweeps across a wide mass range (in your case, m/z 45–200), recording the full mass spectrum at each time point. This is excellent for identification: you get the complete fragmentation pattern and can match it against library databases (like NIST). The downside: sensitivity is lower because the quadrupole spends only a fraction of its time on any single ion.

SIM (Selected Ion Monitoring) mode: Instead of scanning the full range, the quadrupole sits on just a few pre-selected m/z values and monitors them continuously. This dramatically increases sensitivity (10–100× improvement) because the detector spends all its time collecting signal for those specific ions.

Your method uses Scan/SIM: the quadrupole takes turns, one full scan, then the SIM ions, again and again through the whole run. The SIM ions for caffeine are:

• m/z 194, the molecular ion [M]⁺· (quantifier ion, used for quantification)
• m/z 109, a qualifier ion (confirms identity)
• m/z 67, a second qualifier ion

The quantifier ion (194) provides the peak area used for your calibration curve. The qualifier ions (109, 67) are used as a cross-check: if the ratios between the qualifier and quantifier ions in your sample match the ratios in your standard, you can be confident you're actually measuring caffeine and not a co-eluting interferent.

Concept checks. Expand each question below and test your understanding before moving on.
Q Concept check 1: SIM vs scan mode
Why does SIM mode provide higher sensitivity than Scan mode for a target analyte?
SIM increases the electron beam energy above the standard 70 eV, producing more fragment ions per molecule and boosting the overall ion yield at the source
SIM activates an upstream ion gate that physically blocks matrix-derived ions before they reach the quadrupole, reducing chemical noise at the detector
In SIM, the quadrupole spends all its monitoring time on a few selected ions instead of sweeping the entire mass range, collecting more signal per ion
SIM automatically raises the electron multiplier voltage to increase gain, amplifying the signal from target ions while suppressing baseline noise
Correct! Sensitivity is fundamentally about how much time the detector spends collecting signal for your target ion. In Scan mode, the quadrupole rapidly steps through hundreds of m/z values, spending perhaps only 1% of its time on any given ion. In SIM mode, it monitors only a few ions (e.g., 3 for caffeine), so each ion gets ~33% of the total dwell time. More time = more ions counted = better signal-to-noise ratio = lower detection limits. The ionization process and detector gain are identical in both modes.
Q Concept check 2: temperature programming
What role does the temperature program play in your GC method?
It protects the polyimide-coated fused-silica column from thermal shock, since a sudden jump to high temperature would crack the capillary and destroy the stationary phase film
It ensures both low- and high-boiling compounds elute in a reasonable time with good peak shapes, since compounds interact less with the stationary phase at higher temperatures
It thermally decomposes co-extracted matrix interferences at high temperatures, leaving only thermally stable analytes like caffeine to reach the detector intact
It is required to keep helium in the gaseous state throughout the column, since the carrier gas would condense at low oven temperatures and block flow through the capillary
Correct! Without temperature programming, an isothermal run at low temperature would keep high-boiling compounds trapped on the column far too long (producing very broad, flat peaks), while an isothermal run at high temperature would cause all volatile compounds to elute together without separation. The temperature ramp is a compromise: start low for separation of volatiles, then ramp to push higher-boiling compounds off the column efficiently. At higher temperatures, compounds spend more time in the gas phase and less on the stationary phase, speeding their elution.
Answer both concept checks before continuing.

Quantification strategies

Getting a peak on the GC-MS is only half the battle. Turning that signal into a reliable concentration requires careful calibration, and an awareness of what can go wrong.

Work through the numbered sections below in order, then complete the concept checks at the bottom.Work through the screens in order; the concept checks come at the end of the chapter.

You saw peaks like these form in the GC-MS chapter: this is the raw data you need to quantify. The total ion chromatogram (TIC) adds up every ion counted at each moment, so every compound that elutes gives a peak. The mass spectrum at a peak tells you which compound it is.

An extracted ion chromatogram (EIC) shows one m/z only. Extract caffeine’s quantifier ion and the compounds without that ion drop out. A different compound can share the nominal mass, so caffeine’s two qualifier ions must appear at the same retention time, in your standard’s ratios.

Below, step through the peaks and read each one’s spectrum until you find caffeine. Then type its quantifier ion and its two qualifier ions (its spectrum and the GC-MS chapter tell you which) and see where all three line up.

The area of the caffeine peak in its quantifier trace is what you quantify. Where its start, end and baseline go decides that area. Below, pick how the whole calibration curve was auto-integrated, then integrate one of its standards by hand and try to match the auto-integration. Integrate your samples the same way as your standards: consistency is key.

The simplest way to turn a peak area into a concentration is a one-point calibration. You measure a single standard of known concentration and assume that the detector response is directly proportional to concentration, i.e. the calibration line passes through the origin.

csample =
cstandard Āstandard
× Asample

The ratio cstandard / Āstandard is the response factor: how much concentration each unit of peak area represents.

VariableDescription
csampleConcentration of the sample eluate (mg/mL); the unknown you are solving for
cstandardKnown concentration of the caffeine standard (mg/mL)
ĀstandardMean peak area of the three standard injections
AsampleMeasured peak area of the sample eluate

In this experiment, you measure a caffeine standard (c = 0.1 mg/mL) in triplicate at the start of Day 1, before the full calibration curve is ready. After your first sample eluate is measured, you use the one-point equation above to make a rough estimate of the caffeine concentration in your eluate. That estimate is all you need to calculate how much spike to add for the standard spike (target: approximately double the caffeine content).

Why not use this for final quantification? One-point calibration assumes that the calibration line passes through zero (b = 0). In practice, a non-zero y-intercept is common, caused by baseline offsets, chemical noise, or small interferences. Ignoring this intercept introduces systematic error, especially at low concentrations where b can be a significant fraction of the signal. A multi-point calibration curve fits both slope and intercept, and lets you evaluate linearity, identify the working range, and apply weighting if needed [6].

One-point calibration is therefore a useful screening tool for rapid estimates, good enough for calculating your spike volume, but not a substitute for a proper external calibration curve when reporting final results.

In external calibration, you prepare a series of standards with known concentrations of the analyte (caffeine), measure them on the GC-MS, and plot peak area (signal response) versus concentration. The resulting curve is your calibration function.

To determine the concentration in your unknown sample, you measure its peak area and read back the corresponding concentration from the calibration curve. This is the approach you'll use for final quantification in this experiment.

Why "external"? Because the standards are measured in separate injections from your sample, as opposed to internal calibration, where a reference compound is added directly to each sample.

Compared to the one-point estimate, a multi-point curve fits both slope and intercept (y = mx + b) and lets you evaluate linearity across the working range. A linear regression is preferred. If the response is non-linear at high concentrations, a quadratic fit (second-order polynomial) can be used instead. In your experiment report, you'll present the calibration curve including the regression function and R² value.

Below, slide your sample’s peak area and read its concentration off the line. Switch between the one-point estimate, the calibration curve and both together to see where the line through zero goes wrong.

Three features define the quality of a calibration curve:

(1) Number of calibration points: More points = better definition of the regression line. For most bioanalytical work where ±15% accuracy is acceptable, five or six calibrators with two replicates each are a good starting point. You can get away with fewer for a narrow range, but below three points you can't meaningfully define a line.

(2) Placement of points: Ideally, points are spread across the entire expected concentration range. If your sample concentration is very low, adding extra calibrators near the lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) improves accuracy in that critical region.

(3) Replicates: Repeated measurements at each concentration level give you an estimate of precision. More replicates per point = smaller confidence intervals = more reliable predictions. In this lab you replicate only one standard (0.1 mg/mL, injected three times) to get the precision.

Critical rule: Never force your calibration line through zero. The y-intercept is actually diagnostic: a line that naturally passes through zero suggests no interferences; a non-zero intercept could indicate endogenous analyte in your blank or an interfering compound.

Students often rely on R² (the correlation coefficient squared) as the sole indicator of calibration quality. This is insufficient and potentially misleading). Since you're deliberately plotting two variables you already know are related (signal vs. concentration), a high R² is expected and doesn't prove the fit is good [1].

Residuals analysis is much more informative. Residuals are the differences between the measured and predicted values. Plotting them reveals patterns:

• Uniform scatter around zero → good fit, no weighting needed
• Cone-shaped pattern (residuals grow with concentration) → variance is proportional to concentration; apply 1/x weighting
• Curved pattern → linear model is inadequate; consider quadratic regression
• Systematic offset → possible missing variable or calculation error

When the residuals curve: If your residuals form a U-shape instead of scattering randomly, the straight line doesn't fit your data well across the whole range. You could switch to a curved (quadratic) fit, and R² will improve, but that often just papers over the real problem: your detector is saturating at high concentrations. The better fix is to trim your calibration range so it only covers the region where the response is genuinely linear (between the LLOQ and ULOQ). Your protocol allows a quadratic fit "if necessary," but the interactive in section 6 shows why narrowing the range is usually the sounder approach [1, 6].

Why use 1/x weighting? In mass spectrometry, the scatter (variance) around each data point tends to grow as the concentration goes up. An ordinary (unweighted) regression treats every point equally, so high-concentration points with their large scatter end up dominating the fit. The result: the line fits well at the top of the range but poorly at the bottom, exactly where you most need accuracy (your unknown samples often fall near the low end). A 1/x weighting fixes this by giving lower-concentration points more influence in proportion to their concentration. The interactive in section 6 lets you compare unweighted and weighted fits side by side [1].

Every analytical method has boundaries where it becomes unreliable:

Limit of Detection (LOD): The lowest analyte concentration that can be detected, i.e., distinguished from noise with a certain confidence (typically signal-to-noise ratio ≥ 3). You can tell "something is there" but cannot reliably say how much.

Lower Limit of Quantification (LLOQ): The lowest concentration that can be quantified with acceptable accuracy and precision (typically S/N ≥ 10 and ±15–20% accuracy). Below this, your numbers are unreliable.

Upper Limit of Quantification (ULOQ): The highest concentration within the linear (or validated) range. Above this, the detector may saturate, and the relationship between signal and concentration breaks down.

Reporting a concentration below the LLOQ or above the ULOQ without acknowledging it is a major mistake. If your sample concentration falls outside the calibration range, the sample should be diluted (if too high) or concentrated (if too low) and re-measured.

Below, add the standards one at a time, lowest first, and watch each one move the line, R² and the residuals; the zoom window shows the lowest ones. Dots are real data, one injection per standard; diamonds are simulated repeat injections. Switch the residuals to counts to see the scatter grow with concentration, then try a weighting. Tap standards to leave them out until the back-calculated accuracy of every injection is 85–115 % (80–120 % at the lowest): the LLOQ, the ULOQ and the working range between them appear. Then add two saturated standards and see where the range ends.

In this run, leaving out the two lowest and the two saturated standards leaves five good standards, 0.01 to 1 mg/mL. With your own data, let your samples decide. If they all fall between 0.01 and 1 mg/mL, as they should if you calculated your dilutions right, leave out the standards that are not linear and keep at least five. If a sample comes out below 0.01 mg/mL, keep the lower standards: a result only counts inside the range your standards cover.

① Error sources

Sample loss is inherent to the method. No extraction is perfect. Even when every step is performed correctly, some analyte is inevitably lost: not all caffeine binds during loading, small amounts wash off with the polar waste, and elution never strips 100% from the sorbent. These are not mistakes, they are limitations of any real sample preparation workflow. The question is not whether you lose analyte, but how much, and whether you can account for it.

On top of these inherent losses, analytical errors come from the matrix, from the equipment and from how the method performs. These nine are the topics for your flash talk. Human errors are a separate category: avoid them.

Matrix

The drink causes the problem

1  Active sites: matrix compounds cover active sites in the liner, so less caffeine is lost than in clean standards: peaks are bigger and results too high (the slope changes). [7]

2  Co-elution and interferences: a compound at the same retention time either gives the same ions and adds signal (a constant offset), or, at other m/z, suppresses ionization (much less of a problem in EI than in LC-MS). [1, 4]

Equipment

The instrument causes the problem

3  Poor chromatography: tailing, fronting, broad or split peaks and a noisy baseline (column ageing or contamination, overload) make the peak area uncertain. [1]

4  Carryover: residue in the syringe, liner or column appears in the next injection. [1, 4]

5  Instrument drift: the response to the same concentration changes over the overnight sequence (ion source, detector). [1, 4]

Method performance

Calculations of how the method behaved

6  SPE recovery: how much caffeine survives the extraction: breakthrough on loading, incomplete elution, matrix competing for the sorbent. [1, 2]

7  LOD and LOQ: how low the method can detect (LOD) and reliably quantify (LOQ) caffeine; samples near these limits give uncertain results. [1, 6]

8  Calibration model, linearity and range: is the response linear across the calibrated range (0.001–1 mg/mL), or does it bend at the top (detector saturation)? Forcing the line through zero, an unweighted fit across a 1000-fold range, trusting R² alone. [1, 6]

9  Accuracy vs. precision: systematic vs. random error: how close to the true value, and how repeatable. [1]

Human errors

Avoid them; they are not flash-talk topics

• Pipetting errors: especially small volumes (300 µL sample, 50–700 µL spike)

• SPE sorbent running dry: forgetting to close the valve causes loss of retention and low recovery [2, 3]

• Incomplete elution: not enough solvent or eluting too fast leaves caffeine on the cartridge [2]

• Residual water in eluate: poor chromatography, split peaks, and variable peak areas

• Incorrect dilution factors: forgetting your dilution factor or the eluate volume correction

• Contamination: dirty glassware, cross-contamination, or caffeine from skin contact [1]

• Improper standard curve preparation: inaccurate weighing or serial dilution of calibration standards introduces systematic bias into every reported concentration

② Recovery: measuring and correcting for error

To measure how much analyte your method loses, you spike a known amount of caffeine into a separate aliquot of the same sample and put it through a fresh SPE cartridge. The spiked sample’s peak area contains both the original caffeine and the spike. By subtracting the unspiked sample’s contribution (corrected for elution volume), the remainder is what you recovered from the spike [1].

Before writing the recovery equation, you need three building blocks:

Concentration from the calibration curve

Your calibration curve relates peak area (A) to concentration. Rearranging y = mx + b gives:

c =
A − b m

This gives cspiked (spiked eluate) and csample (unspiked sample eluate), both in mg/mL.

Volume from gravimetric measurement

Volumetric pipettes are imprecise for small organic-solvent volumes. Instead, weigh the collection tube before and after elution and convert using the density of acetonitrile (ρACN = 0.782 g/mL):

V =
mtube+eluate − mtube ρACN

This gives Vspiked (spiked eluate volume) and Vsample (unspiked sample eluate volume), both in mL.

Expected spike concentration

Unlike cspiked and csample, cspike,exp is not read from the calibration curve. You know exactly how much caffeine standard you spiked in, so the expected concentration in the spiked eluate is:

cspike,exp =
mspike Vspiked

where mspike is the mass of caffeine standard added (mg) and Vspiked is the spiked eluate volume (mL).

Putting it all together:

Recovery (%) =
cspiked · Vspiked − csample · Vsample cspike,exp · Vspiked
× 100

The numerator is the mass of recovered spike (spiked total minus sample background). The denominator is the mass of spike you expected to find if nothing were lost.

VariableDescription
cspikedConcentration of the spiked eluate (mg/mL), from the calibration curve
csampleConcentration of the unspiked sample eluate (mg/mL), from the calibration curve
cspike,expExpected spike concentration = mspike / Vspiked (known, not from the cal curve)
VspikedSpiked eluate volume (mL), measured gravimetrically
VsampleUnspiked sample eluate volume (mL), measured gravimetrically

Below, set how much caffeine the SPE loses and how much the matrix boosts the signal, or leave wash water in one tube, and watch the recovery and the drink value it corrects.

Acceptable recovery is typically 80 to 120%. Values outside this range indicate systematic loss (low recovery) or matrix enhancement (high recovery).

On a GC, matrix enhancement comes from active sites: exposed Si–OH groups in the hot liner and at the start of the column that hold caffeine back, as a late tail or for good. Compounds from the drink occupy these sites first, so the same caffeine gives a bigger peak than in a neat standard [7]. Below, three standards, each scaled to its own peak as the software shows it. Change how many sites the drink covers.

Because the spike sits in the same matrix as the analyte, the matrix effect acts on both equally. Standard spiking therefore corrects for both SPE losses and matrix effects at once. However, each aliquot is a physically different sample with its own pipetting, extraction, and transfer variability. Standard spiking does not correct for operator errors that differ between the spiked and unspiked aliquots.

③ Internal standards: a better correction

An internal standard (IS) is a co-eluting isotope-labelled compound added to every sample before preparation begins. Because the IS travels through the entire workflow alongside the analyte, both experience the same losses. Their ratio stays constant, correcting for recovery / sample loss, matrix effects, detector drift, and all operator errors that occur after the IS is added. It even partially compensates for integration errors, since the IS peak is usually mis-integrated in the same way as the analyte peak. It does not fix isobaric interferences or a wrong calibration model [1].

If an internal standard corrects for so much more than standard spiking, why do you think we didn’t use one in this experiment?

Concept checks. Expand each question below and test your understanding before moving on.
Q Concept check 1: evaluating R²
You run a calibration curve and get R² = 0.998. A colleague tells you "the calibration is perfect." Why should you be skeptical?
R² only measures correlation strength, not fit quality; a high value is expected by design and residuals analysis is needed to reveal problems like nonlinearity
An R² of 0.998 exceeds the theoretical maximum for mass spectrometry data, which suggests the standards were measured multiple times and averaged to artificially reduce variance
R² is only valid for spectrophotometric detectors with linear Beer–Lambert responses; for mass spectrometry data, the Mandel fitting test should be used instead
Any R² below 1.000 indicates the calibration has failed, because a properly prepared standard series with no pipetting errors should produce a perfect linear fit
Correct! This is a commonly misunderstood point. As Gale and Duncan emphasize, using R² as a figure of merit for a calibration curve is statistically inappropriate because the two variables are not independently varying. You intentionally created a relationship between them. A high R² is essentially guaranteed and tells you nothing about whether the model is correct. Residuals analysis reveals whether the variance is homogeneous, whether the relationship is truly linear, and whether weighting is needed. A "perfect" R² can hide serious problems that only become visible in a residuals plot.
Q Concept check 2: forcing through zero
Why is the calibration line never forced through zero?
Because detector electronic noise always produces a nonzero baseline signal, so a blank measurement can never truly read zero and the origin is not a valid data point
Because most chromatography data systems use ordinary least-squares algorithms that mathematically cannot constrain the intercept to zero without switching to a weighted model
Because the y-intercept is diagnostically useful: it can reveal interferences or endogenous analyte, and forcing through zero distorts the regression
Because removing the intercept term from the linear model causes the slope to become undefined, making it mathematically impossible to solve the regression equation
Correct! The y-intercept of the calibration curve is a diagnostic tool. If the regression line naturally passes through (or near) zero, that's a good sign: it suggests no interferences contribute to the signal at the analyte's retention time. If the intercept is significantly non-zero, it could indicate: (1) endogenous analyte in the blank matrix, (2) a co-eluting interferent contributing to the signal, or (3) contamination. Forcing through zero eliminates this diagnostic and artificially distorts the regression, particularly biasing low-concentration predictions.
Answer both concept checks, then take every calculation along on one page.
